title-group.article-title: Parameters associated with the size of the foveal avascular zone in healthy elderly eyes

abstract.p: To determine parameters related to the size of the foveal avascular zone (FAZ) in healthy elderly eyes. We reviewed the medical records of 101 normal elderly eyes with a mean age of 64.2 ± 10.1 years. A 3 × 3 mm area centered on the fovea was analyzed in optical coherence tomography angiographic images. The center of FAZ and the center of foveal photoreceptors were identified, and the misalignment between the two center points was measured. The mean FAZ size was 0.35 ± 0.12 mm2. The distance between the center of the FAZ and the center of the foveal photoreceptors was 41.6 ± 21.1 μm. The misalignment distance between the center of the FAZ and the center of the foveal photoreceptors was not significantly correlated with the size of the FAZ (r = 0.091, P = 0.3656). On the other hand, there was a significant correlation between the directionality of horizontal and vertical misalignments from the center of the foveal photoreceptors to the center of the FAZ and the FAZ size (r = -0.264, P = 0.0076 horizontal; r = 0.212, P = 0.0335, vertical). These results indicate that the larger the misalignment of the center of the FAZ from the center of the foveal photoreceptors in the temporal and superior directions, the larger the FAZ tended to be. In conclusion, analysis of parameters related to FAZ size in healthy elderly eyes may provide clues to age-related changes in macular microcirculation and early pathology in eyes with retinal diseases.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The fovea is a highly specialized region of the human retina that is responsible for the highest visual acuity. It is characterized by a foveal avascular zone (FAZ), absence of the inner retinal layers, increased cone density, and elongation of the photoreceptor outer segments1–3. Previous studies of the macula have used fluorescein angiography and focused primarily on the macular microvasculature and FAZ4,5. The introduction of optical coherence tomography (OCT) has allowed clinicians to assess the status of the outer retinal microstructures at the fovea. The integrity of these microstructures has been shown to be a good marker of retinal disease6–8. The advent of OCT angiography (OCTA) made it possible to noninvasively evaluate the microvascular network in en-face images and allowed clinicians to analyze the morphology of the FAZ in greater detail. In diseased eyes, such as those with diabetic retinopathy, an enlarged FAZ and a decrease in the circularity of the FAZ have been reported9,10. It has also been reported that analyses of the FAZ are essential for the evaluation of visual functions11. However, the size of the FAZ has been reported to vary considerably, even among normal eyes12–15. Factors associated with FAZ area include age, gender, macular retinal thickness, and macular morphology12–15.

Careful examination of the structural OCT images of normal eyes has shown that the ellipsoid zone has a bulge at the central fovea, called the foveal bulge. It has been reported that the presence or absence of a foveal bulge is significantly correlated with the visual acuity in several ocular diseases16–18. Thus, the center of the foveal bulge is considered the center of the foveal photoreceptors. Recently, our OCTA and structural OCT study showed that the misalignment of the center of the foveal bulge to the center of the FAZ was greater in eyes with epiretinal membrane than in normal eyes19. We also found that there was a small distance of 38.7 ± 20.0 μm between the center of the FAZ and the center of the foveal bulge even in the normal eyes19.By focusing on this misalignment, it was possible to evaluate not only the size and circularity of the FAZ, but also the misalignment of the FAZ in the horizontal and vertical directions. These results will provide new information about the morphology of the FAZ in normal eyes.
Therefore, the purpose of this study was to analyze the morphology of the FAZ in healthy elderly eyes and to determine the factors associated with the variations in the size of the FAZ.

sec.title: Macular microstructures in healthy elderly eyes
sec.p: The macular characteristics of the eyes are summarized in Table 1. The mean age was 64.2 ± 10.1 years. The mean FAZ size was 0.35 ± 0.12 mm2, the mean FAZ circularity was 0.78 ± 0.05. The mean 1-mm central subfield thickness (CST) was 251.5 ± 20.8 μm. The distance between the center of the FAZ and the center of the foveal bulge was 41.6 ± 21.1 μm. The center of the FAZ was located 13.0 ± 31.6 μm temporally and 3.7 ± 31.8 μm inferiorly to the center of the foveal bulge (Fig. 1).

sec.title: Associations of the size of the FAZ and the clinical characteristics
sec.p: The associations between the size of the FAZ and the clinical characteristics of the healthy elderly eyes are shown in Fig. 2. The CST was significantly correlated with the size of the FAZ (r = −0.701, P < 0.0001). The distance between the center of FAZ and the center of foveal bulge was not significantly correlated with the size of the FAZ (r = 0.091, P = 0.3656). On the other hand, the size of the FAZ was found to be related to the directionality of horizontal and vertical misalignments from the center of the foveal bulge to the center of the FAZ (r = −0.264, P = 0.0076 horizontal; r = 0.212, P = 0.0335, vertical). These findings indicated that the size of the FAZ tended to be larger and the center of the FAZ was more temporal and superior to the center of the foveal bulge.

caption.p: Scatter plot showing the relationship between the size of the foveal avascular zone (FAZ) and each parameter. The horizontal and vertical misalignment from the center of the foveal bulge to the center of the FAZ were determined with the center of the foveal bulge as the reference point (a-g). The central subfield thickness was significantly correlated with the size of the FAZ. The horizontal and vertical misalignment of the center of the FAZ from the center of the foveal bulge were also significantly correlated with the size of the FAZ.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The results showed that there was no significant correlation between the FAZ size and the foveal misalignment distance, but there was a significant correlation between the directionality of horizontal and vertical misalignments from the center of the foveal bulge to the center of the FAZ and the FAZ size. In other words, the larger the misalignment of the center of the FAZ from the center of the foveal bulge in the temporal and superior directions, the larger the FAZ tended to be; cases with larger FAZ are not concentrically larger from the center of the foveal bulge, but directionally larger temporally and superiorly. The reason why the center of the FAZ tends to be misaligned temporally and superiorly from the center of the foveal bulge in eyes with a large FAZ size is not clear, but two types of changes may be involved: those occurring during fovea maturation and those associated with aging.

In the human retina, blood vessels begin to form at the optic disc at around 14 weeks’ gestation, blood vessel formation occurs relatively slowly along the temporal horizontal meridian, while those superior and inferior skirt around the incipient fovea20,21. Blood vessels form a complex meshwork on the nasal side of the developing fovea at 26 weeks’ gestation, while on the temporal side, blood vessels are still separated into superior and inferior lobes along the horizontal meridian. By 37 weeks’ gestation, these lobes have fused, and the early fovea is encircled by fine blood vessels to form the FAZ20,21. In the vascular ring surrounding the fovea, this is caused by the fusion of the superior and inferior vessels on the temporal side, and in cases with larger FAZ size, the center of the FAZ may be more likely to deviate toward the temporal side. Next, the perfusion flow may be associated with the microcirculatory changes that occur with aging. According to the Hagen-Poiseuille law, flow rate is proportional to inversely correlated to the length of the vessel22,23. Therefore, an imbalance in perfusion flow is more likely to occur in the temporal region of the macula than in the nasal region because the temporal region is farther from the optic disc. In eyes with diabetic retinopathy, a recent OCTA study showed that parafoveal capillary dropout was significantly more common in the superior and temporal quadrants than in the inferior and nasal quadrants over a one-year period24. A previous study using OCT images showed that the superior quadrant retina tends to be thicker than the inferior quadrant retina in healthy eyes25,26. The superior side retina may be more susceptible to nutritional supply-demand imbalances because the retina requires greater amounts of oxygen and glucose in the superior side than in the inferior side. Thus, similar microvascular changes may occur not only in diseased eyes but also in normal eyes with aging. Furthermore, Nesmith and associates mathematically analyzed foveal OCT images of 390 normal eyes aged 13 to 97 years and reported that the younger fovea was more symmetrical along the midline, but the older fovea was significantly less symmetrical along the midline27. Thus, the foveal morphology, which is not significantly symmetrical along the midline, may be related to the fact that the center of the FAZ tends to deviate temporally and superiorly from the center of the foveal bulge.

Our study showed that the CST was significantly and negatively correlated with the size of the FAZ. This result is consistent with the findings of previous studies14,15,28,29. Previous studies have reported that the terminal microvessels of the FAZ are located within the inner nuclear layer (INL), near its boundary with the inner plexiform layer30,31. This suggests a close relationship between the INL free zone and the FAZ area. A deep foveal pit is associated with a thinner central retinal thickness, a wider INL free zone, and a larger FAZ. In contrast, a shallow foveal pit is associated with thicker central retinal thickness, a narrower INL free zone, and a smaller FAZ14,15,28–33.

This study has several limitations. First, this was a retrospective study with its inherent sampling bias. In this study, FAZ morphology was analyzed only in eyes older than 50 years with no macular abnormalities. Furthermore, this was a cross-sectional study and it was not possible to evaluate changes in FAZ over time. Elucidation of changes in the FAZ over time in normal eyes would be useful in the interpretation of various pathologic conditions. Therefore, it will be necessary in the future to evaluate age-related changes in the FAZ in a larger number of normal eyes, from young to elderly, and also to evaluate changes in FAZ morphology over time in normal elderly eyes. Second, this study examined the distance and directionality of misalignment between the center of the foveal bulge and the center of the FAZ. Since foveal position correlates with cyclotorsion, this factor may influence it. This study took care to keep the face straight during OCTA imaging to prevent tilting.

In conclusion, our study showed that the larger the misalignment of the center of the FAZ from the center of the foveal bulge in the temporal and superior directions, the larger the FAZ tended to be. Thus, analysis of parameters related to FAZ size in healthy elderly eyes may provide new insights into age-related changes in macular microcirculation and early pathology in eyes with retinal diseases.

sec.title: Participants
sec.p: This was a cross-sectional, retrospective study. On October 3, 2017, the Institutional Review Board of Tokyo Women’s Medical University Hospital approved the retrospective review of participants’ medical records (ID 2636-R). The procedures used in this study conformed to the tenets of the Declaration of Helsinki. This study was conducted exclusively on the fellow eye with no observed fundus abnormalities among cases undergoing vitrectomy for unilateral epiretinal membrane at Tokyo Women’s Medical University Hospital between April 2020 and March 2023. Informed consent for the retrospective review of all examinations and medical records was obtained from all participants. This study ultimately included 101 eyes of individuals aged 50 years or older who had a best-corrected visual acuity ≥ 20/20 and an axial length between 22 and less than 30 mm. Eyes with other intraocular diseases, such as diabetic retinopathy, age-related macular degeneration, uveitis, epiretinal membrane, vitreomacular traction syndrome, severe cataract, or previous vitreoretinal surgery were excluded. Eyes with poor quality OCTA images (scan quality < 7/10) and with tilted structural OCT images were also excluded due to the unreliability of the FAZ measurements.

sec.title: FAZ size measurement and determination of the center of FAZ and the center of foveal bulge
sec.p: OCTA images were obtained with the AngioVue system (Avanti; Optovue Inc, Fremont, California, USA). A 3 × 3 mm area centered on the fovea was scanned, and the OCTA slab containing the retina from the ILM to 9 μm below the outer plexiform layer was analyzed as a full layer of the retina. The FAZ size was quantitatively using AngioAnalytics software (version: 2018.0.0.18).

The centroid is the center of a two-dimensional figure. ImageJ software (version: 1.54 g, NIH, Bethesda, Maryland, USA, https://imagej.net/ij/download.html) was then used to calculate the centroid as the center of the FAZ. The circularity of the FAZ was measured using ImageJ software as an indicator of its accuracy as a circle. A value close to 1 indicates a perfect circle. In normal eyes, the structural OCT images showed that the ellipsoid zone had a bulge in the central fovea16–18. The foveal bulge is thought to be related to the morphologic specificity of the foveal photoreceptors. Therefore, we determined the location of this OCT finding and labeled it as the center of the foveal photoreceptors. The distance from the center of the foveal bulge to the center of the FAZ was then determined using ImageJ software. In addition, the distribution of distances between the center of the FAZ and the center of the foveal bulge was determined using the center of the foveal bulge as the reference point (Fig. 3). If the center of the FAZ was located temporal to the center of the foveal bulge, its value was considered a minus value, and if it was located nasally, its value was considered a plus value. If the center of the FAZ was located superiorly to the center of the foveal bulge, its value was considered a plus value and if it was located inferiorly, its value was considered a minus value.

caption.p: Misalignment measurements between the center of the foveal avascular zone and the center of the foveal bulge using optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA). (a) The intersection of the red and green lines indicates the center of the foveal bulge of the ellipsoid zone. The white dot indicates the center of the FAZ, and it is located at the centroid of the FAZ. (b) Magnified view of white dotted line surroundings. If the center of the FAZ was temporal to the center of the foveal bulge, its value was considered a minus value, and if it was nasal, it was considered a plus value. If the center of the FAZ was superior to the center of the foveal bulge, its value was considered a plus value, and if it was inferior, its value was considered a minus value.

sec.title: Correction of OCTA parameters by axial length
sec.p: The Littman and modified Bennett formulas were used to calculate the true image size, as described previously34–37. Briefly, the relationship between the measured OCTA image diameter (Dm) and the true fundus diameter (Dt) could be expressed as Dt = p × q × Dm, where p is the magnification factor of the imaging system and q is an eye-related factor (q = 0.01306 × [axial length − 1.82]). For the Avanti systems used, the value of the magnification factor (p) was 3.46 for a nominal axial length of 23.95 mm38. Using this equation, Dt can be calculated as Dt = 3.46 × 0.01306 × (axial length − 1.82) × Dm. This correction formula was used to correct the distance from the center of the foveal bulge to the center of the FAZ, the horizontal misalignment, and the vertical misalignment of the center of the FAZ from the center of the foveal bulge. The corrected FAZ area was then calculated using the formula: corrected FAZ area = FAZ area × 3.462 × 0.013062 × (axial length − 1.82)2.

sec.title: Statistical analyses
sec.p: The correlation between the size of the FAZ and the clinical parameters was determined by Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient. A P value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. All analyses were performed with the JMP (version Pro 18; SAS Institute, Cary, North Carolina, USA). To determine the appropriate sample size for analyzing correlations, a power calculation was performed at a significance level of 0.05 and a power of 0.8. This yielded an n value of 64.74. This study examined 101 eyes, which is a sufficient sample size to meet the required power.
